title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 malicious release (PyPI + Docker) steals credentials via cook.pth
summary: Attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens to publish litellm 1.107.0 to PyPI and Docker; a cook.pth file runs a credential stealer at every Python start (even if litellm is never imported) and a backdoor polls a GitHub dead drop hourly, so any environment that installed or ran it must be treated as compromised.
notes: Pulled from PyPI/Docker within ~2-3h; LiteLLM revoked tokens. Docker tags latest, main-latest and main-stable also pointed at the bad build during the window (bad digest per Brandefense: sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e). 1.107.0rc1/rc2 reported clean by SafeDep. A March 2026 LiteLLM compromise (TeamPCP campaign) used the same cook.pth start-up trick. Lookalike GitHub org Berri-AI/litellm (real: BerriAI/litellm).

files.meaning: Start-up hook: runs the stealer every time this Python starts
The malicious release was installed into this environment
Linked to the backdoor daemon in this campaign; some legitimate setups also ship one, so read it
Backdoor (C2 loader) daemon ran or is still running

remediation.why: LiteLLM is often a transitive dependency; the .pth runs even if your code never imports it.
remediation.danger: Do not run pip/python inside a suspect environment to check it: every Python start re-runs cook.pth. Use python -S (skips .pth processing) or plain file search.

windows: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -Filter cook.pth -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName
any: grep -rn 'litellm' uv.lock poetry.lock Pipfile.lock requirements*.txt 2>/dev/null | grep '1.107.0'

remediation.step: Contain: stop the backdoor and quarantine the start-up files
remediation.why: Stops the hourly C2 poll and stops re-theft of the new secrets you are about to create.
remediation.danger: Do this before rotating secrets, or the stealer can grab the new ones on the next Python start.

any: Block egress to litellm.dev at DNS/firewall

remediation.step: Rotate every secret the host could read, from a clean machine
remediation.why: The stealer took cloud tokens, SSH keys, AI tool credentials, browser data, env vars and LiteLLM proxy keys/config.
remediation.danger: Rotate from a different, clean machine. Only revoke after the old creds are replaced in your apps, and check audit logs before deleting anything.

any: List: cloud keys and instance/task roles, LLM provider keys stored in the LiteLLM proxy, LiteLLM master + virtual keys, proxy DB password, GitHub/gh tokens, SSH keys, AI tool credentials, browser sessions, every .env value

remediation.step: Rebuild the environment on 1.106.2 pinned by hash/digest
remediation.why: Upgrading in place keeps leftovers (sitecustomize.py, cook.*); a fresh env is the clean fix.
remediation.danger: Deleting the old venv/container is your call; keep a copy in quarantine if you want forensics.

any: pip install 'litellm==1.106.2'   # in a NEW venv; then lock with hashes: pip-compile --generate-hashes / uv lock
docker pull ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:<1.106.2-tag> && docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:<1.106.2-tag>   # then reference image@sha256:... in compose/k8s
Rebuild CI runners and proxy containers that ran 1.107.0

remediation.why: Confirms what left the host and whether stolen creds were used elsewhere.

any: Search proxy/DNS/firewall logs for litellm.dev, /healthcheck and /codepy
Review cloud audit logs for use of rotated keys from unknown IPs
Check every CI runner and image built 2026-10-21

remediation.step: Harden installs against the next poisoned release
remediation.why: Hash/digest pins stop a re-published tag from silently changing what you run.

any: Lock Python deps with hashes (uv.lock, pip-compile --generate-hashes, pip install --require-hashes)
Pin images by @sha256 digest, never latest/main-latest/main-stable
Add a release cooldown before adopting brand-new versions
